ask: What weaknesses does the BRISK report acknowledge?
rows.text:
s1 = Research/BRISK trial report.pdf @adc17a3fac6d
[1] s1 text:
  p.1 BRISK: a randomised trial of a home exercise programme for knee osteoarthritis
  p.1 Background: Knee osteoarthritis is a leading cause of pain and disability in older adults. We tested whether a 12-week home exercise programme reduces pain compared with usual care. Methods: We randomised 412 adults aged 50 to 79 with painful knee osteoarthritis to the home exercise programme or usual care at six community clinics. Results: At 12 weeks, pain improved by 2.1 points more with exercise than with usual care on the 20-point WOMAC pain scale. Function also improved. Conclusions: A home exercise programme reduces knee pain in the short term.
  p.1 Exercise is recommended for knee osteoarthritis, but supervised classes are costly and many people do not attend them. Home programmes could reach more people at lower cost. Previous trials of home programmes were small and followed participants for less than three months.
  p.2 Participants were recruited from six community clinics between March 2023 and February 2024. Eligible adults were aged 50 to 79, had knee pain on most days for at least three months, and had radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis. People with a knee replacement planned within six months were excluded.
  p.2 Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio, stratified by clinic, to the home exercise programme (n=206) or usual care (n=206). The programme consisted of eight strengthening exercises performed three times a week, with two physiotherapist visits and a printed booklet.
  p.2 The primary outcome was the change in WOMAC pain score (0 to 20, higher is worse) from baseline to 12 weeks. Secondary outcomes were WOMAC function (0 to 68), adherence recorded in exercise diaries, and adverse events. Participants were followed up at 12 and 24 weeks.
  p.2 The minimal clinically important difference for WOMAC pain was taken as 1.5 points. Analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle.
  p.2 Assuming a standard deviation of 4.2 points for the change in WOMAC pain, 186 participants per group gave 90% power to detect the minimal clinically important difference at a two-sided significance level of 5%. Allowing for 10% loss to follow-up, we planned to randomise 412 participants.
  p.2 The primary analysis used a linear mixed model with group, clinic and baseline pain as fixed effects. Missing outcomes were handled by multiple imputation with 20 imputed data sets under a missing-at-random assumption, and a complete-case analysis was done as a sensitivity analysis. Pre-specified subgroup analyses examined sex and baseline pain severity. Secondary outcomes were analysed with the same model, without adjustment for multiplicity, and are reported as estimates with confidence intervals.
  p.2 An independent data monitoring committee reviewed safety data after 100 and 250 participants had completed 12 weeks. No interim analysis of effectiveness was planned.
  p.3 We screened 1,083 people, of whom 671 were not eligible or declined: 288 had pain on fewer than half of days, 141 had a joint replacement planned, 97 could not commit to the programme and 145 declined for other reasons.
  p.3 Of 412 participants randomised, 377 (92%) completed the 12-week assessment and 351 (85%) completed the 24-week assessment. Baseline characteristics were similar in the two groups; the mean age was 64 years and 58% were women.
  p.3 At 12 weeks, the mean WOMAC pain score fell by 3.1 points in the exercise group and by 1.4 points in the usual care group, a difference of 1.7 points (95% CI 0.9 to 2.5). This difference exceeded the minimal clinically important difference.
  p.3 Function improved more with exercise than with usual care (Table 2). Adherence to the programme was 71% over 12 weeks, measured as the share of prescribed sessions recorded in diaries.
  p.4 Table 2. Secondary outcomes at 12 weeks
  p.4 Benefits were smaller among participants aged 70 and over, in whom the difference in pain was 0.6 points. Benefits did not differ by sex. However, the age subgroup analysis was not pre-specified, and its confidence interval included zero.
  p.4 Most adverse events were mild muscle soreness that resolved within a week; one participant in the exercise group had a fall that required a clinic visit.
  p.5 At 24 weeks, the difference in pain between groups had narrowed to 0.8 points (95% CI -0.1 to 1.6) and was no longer statistically significant. Adherence fell to 48% between weeks 12 and 24.
  p.5 A home exercise programme reduced knee pain at 12 weeks by more than the minimal clinically important difference, but the effect waned by 24 weeks as adherence declined. Booster sessions might sustain the benefit.
  p.5 Our findings are consistent with a supervised exercise trial by Okafor and colleagues, which reported a 2.4-point reduction in WOMAC pain at 12 weeks, and with a meta-analysis of 31 trials that found a mean difference of 1.9 points.
  p.5 The programme required little staff time: two physiotherapist visits and a booklet. If its short-term benefit can be sustained, it could be offered in primary care at modest cost. Participants who completed most sessions reported the largest improvements, but this comparison is not randomised and may reflect healthier participants adhering more.
  p.5 Our participants were recruited from community clinics in one region and most were White, so the results may not apply to other settings. People with severe pain or planned joint replacement were excluded.
  p.6 Participants and physiotherapists were not blinded to group allocation, and pain was self-reported, which may have exaggerated the benefit. Adherence was measured with diaries rather than activity monitors. The trial was not powered to detect differences in adverse events.
  p.6 We thank the clinic staff and participants. The trial was funded by the Northern Health Research Fund, which had no role in the analysis. Statistical analysis used R version 4.3.

  p.1 Riparian Buffer Restoration and Stream Water Quality in the Halden Vale
  p.1 Final monitoring report, 2021 to 2024. Prepared by the monitoring team of the Halden Vale Rivers Trust for the Halden Catchment Partnership. Report HVRT-MR-25-02, March 2025.
  p.1 Reviewed by the Partnership's technical group in February 2025. Distribution: Partnership members, participating landowners and the regulator's catchment team.
  p.1 Diffuse pollution from livestock farming is the main pressure on the tributaries of the River Halden. Between January and March 2022 the Halden Catchment Partnership fenced cattle and sheep out of six tributary reaches and planted native broadleaf woodland buffers 10 to 30 metres wide along both banks. We sampled these six restored reaches and six matched control reaches every month from January 2021 to December 2024 in a before-after-control-impact (BACI) design, comparing the 2021 baseline year with 2024, the third growing season after planting. Mean nitrate-N concentrations at restored reaches fell by 31% between 2021 and 2024, while concentrations at control reaches changed little. Total phosphorus and storm-event turbidity also declined at restored reaches, and the mean macroinvertebrate community index rose by 0.7 points. Responses were strongest where buffers were at least 20 metres wide. We conclude that woodland buffers of this width are an effective way to reduce nitrate in lowland livestock catchments, and we recommend widening buffers narrower than 20 metres where land can be secured.
  p.1 Keywords: riparian buffer; diffuse pollution; nitrate; phosphorus; turbidity; stream temperature; macroinvertebrates; BACI design.
  p.2 The River Halden drains about 21,000 hectares of lowland farmland, roughly two thirds of it grazed grassland. Its tributaries have failed their nutrient standards in every classification since 2015, mainly because nitrate and phosphorus are washed from fields and released where livestock have direct access to the channel. Riparian buffers, strips of permanent vegetation between farmland and the stream, are widely promoted as a low-cost remedy because they intercept runoff, take up nutrients, stabilise banks and shade the water. Their performance in practice varies a great deal, however, and few schemes have been monitored for long enough, or against suitable controls, to separate the effect of the buffer from changes in weather and farming.
  p.2 In 2021 the Partnership agreed to fund buffer planting on six tributary reaches and asked the Trust to find out whether water quality and stream ecology improved as a result. This report presents the full four years of monitoring. It addresses three questions: whether nutrient concentrations and turbidity fell at restored reaches relative to controls; whether conditions for stream invertebrates improved; and whether the response depended on the width of the buffer.
  p.2 Published evaluations report a wide range of outcomes. In a review of 38 buffer schemes in temperate Europe, Ostrander and Vey (2018) found a median nitrate reduction of 33% in shallow groundwater beneath buffers but only 12% in the receiving streams. On the Kell Water, nitrate-N fell from 6.1 to 4.9 mg/L in the ten years after a 15-metre grass buffer was established, a reduction of 20%, with no change in total phosphorus (Brennan and colleagues, 2017). Wooded buffers in the Ardle uplands, by contrast, reduced total phosphorus by 27% within three years (Haldane and Pike, 2020).
  p.2 Shading effects are better established. Summer maximum water temperatures beneath a mature riparian canopy are typically 2 to 4 °C lower than in open reaches (Maddox, 2015), and newly planted buffers have lowered summer maxima by 0.8 °C within five years (Ferrar and Quine, 2021). Invertebrate responses tend to lag behind chemical change: Ostrander and Vey (2018) reported that community index scores rose by 0.4 points on average, and only in schemes more than five years old. Several authors conclude that buffers narrower than 10 metres deliver little benefit for nitrate (Brennan and colleagues, 2017; Okoro, 2019).
  p.3 Twelve reaches, each 500 metres long, were selected on eight first- and second-order tributaries. Six were restored and six served as controls. Control reaches were matched to restored reaches on upstream catchment area, share of grazed grassland and baseline nitrate concentration, and none was fenced or planted during the study. At restored reaches, livestock were excluded with post-and-wire fencing, and the strip between the fence and the bank top was planted at 2,500 trees per hectare with alder, willow, hawthorn and oak. Duplicate samples and field blanks were analysed with every batch, and all batches met the laboratory's acceptance criteria. Temperature loggers recorded water temperature every 15 minutes from May to September. Macroinvertebrates were sampled each October with a three-minute kick sample and scored on the community index used by the regional regulator, on which higher scores indicate cleaner water.

  p.1 Evaluation of the Northfold Community Pharmacy Stop-Smoking Programme
  p.1 Twelve-month results of a cluster-randomised trial. Final report to Northfold Council Public Health, November 2024. Prepared by the Northfold Health Services Evaluation Unit.
  p.1 Background: Most smokers who try to stop do so without professional help, and specialist stop-smoking clinics reach few of them. Community pharmacies are open long hours and are visited by many smokers, which makes them a promising place to offer structured support.
  p.1 Methods: Twenty-four community pharmacies were randomly allocated to deliver the programme (12 pharmacies) or usual care (12 pharmacies). The programme offered six weekly one-to-one sessions with a trained pharmacy adviser and up to 12 weeks of free varenicline or combination nicotine replacement therapy. Usual care consisted of brief advice and a referral to the council's telephone quitline. The primary outcome was continuous abstinence from smoking at 52 weeks, confirmed by an exhaled carbon monoxide reading below 10 parts per million.
  p.1 Results: Between March 2022 and February 2023, 2,310 adult smokers enrolled, 1,212 at programme pharmacies and 1,098 at usual-care pharmacies. At 52 weeks, 14.2% of programme participants and 8.9% of usual-care participants were abstinent (adjusted odds ratio 1.71, 95% confidence interval 1.26 to 2.32). The programme also increased validated abstinence at four weeks.
  p.1 Conclusions: Structured support from a trained pharmacy adviser, with free stop-smoking medicine, increased long-term quitting compared with brief advice. Community pharmacies are a practical setting for stop-smoking support in Northfold.
  p.2 About 17% of adults in Northfold smoke, above the regional average, and smoking remains the largest single cause of the gap in life expectancy between the most and least deprived parts of the district. The council's specialist stop-smoking clinic sees around 600 smokers a year, a small fraction of those who try to quit. In 2021 the council commissioned a pharmacy-based programme to reach more smokers and asked the Evaluation Unit to test it against usual care before deciding whether to extend it across the district.
  p.2 Evidence on pharmacy-delivered support is mixed. A national audit of pharmacy stop-smoking services found an average four-week quit rate of 35%, although fewer than half of the reported quits were confirmed by carbon monoxide testing (Lomax, 2019). In a cluster trial in 16 pharmacies in Tayford, Ridley and colleagues (2020) reported continuous abstinence at 52 weeks of 11.5% with behavioural support plus nicotine replacement therapy, against 7.2% with brief advice.
  p.2 Medication choice matters. In specialist clinics, varenicline has produced 52-week continuous abstinence of around 23%, compared with 16% for combination nicotine replacement (Ashworth and Nair, 2016). Results for heavier smokers are less consistent: one trial found that smokers of 20 or more cigarettes a day were half as likely as lighter smokers to remain abstinent at 52 weeks (Kerr, 2018), while another found no difference by smoking level (Duval and Haas, 2021). Few trials have reported results separately for older smokers.
  p.3 This was a pragmatic cluster-randomised trial. All 41 community pharmacies in Northfold were invited, and 24 agreed to take part. Pharmacies were randomised in pairs matched on monthly prescription volume and local deprivation, with 12 allocated to the programme and 12 to usual care. Randomisation was carried out by a statistician who had no contact with the pharmacies.
  p.3 Pharmacy staff invited customers who smoked to take part. Adults aged 18 or over who smoked at least five cigarettes a day and wanted to stop within the next month were eligible. Pregnant women were not eligible, because they are referred to the specialist maternity stop-smoking service, and people already using a stop-smoking medicine were also excluded.
  p.3 3.3 Programme and usual care
  p.3 In programme pharmacies, a trained adviser offered six weekly one-to-one sessions of about 20 minutes, starting one week before the quit date. Advisers were pharmacy staff who had completed a two-day accredited training course. Participants chose either varenicline or combination nicotine replacement therapy (a patch plus a short-acting product), supplied free for up to 12 weeks. In usual-care pharmacies, staff gave brief advice and a written referral to the council's telephone quitline, and customers could buy nicotine replacement products as normal.
  p.3 The primary outcome was self-reported continuous abstinence from two weeks after the quit date to 52 weeks, allowing no more than five cigarettes in total, confirmed by an exhaled carbon monoxide reading below 10 parts per million. Secondary outcomes were carbon monoxide-validated abstinence at four weeks and self-reported seven-day abstinence at 26 weeks. Participants lost to follow-up were counted as smokers. Groups were compared with logistic regression adjusted for pharmacy pair, age, sex and cigarettes per day, with standard errors allowing for clustering by pharmacy. Subgroup analyses by cigarettes per day (fewer than 20, or 20 or more) and by sex were specified in advance.
  p.4 Between March 2022 and February 2023, 2,310 smokers enrolled: 1,212 at programme pharmacies and 1,098 at usual-care pharmacies. The two groups were similar at enrolment (Table 1). Participants had a mean age of 44 years, 52% were women, and they smoked a mean of 17 cigarettes a day. Programme pharmacies enrolled a median of 98 participants each and usual-care pharmacies a median of 89. Follow-up at 52 weeks was completed by 78% of programme participants and 73% of usual-care participants.

  p.1 Evaluation of the Northfold Community Pharmacy Stop-Smoking Programme
  p.1 Twelve-month results of a cluster-randomised trial. Final report to Northfold Council Public Health, November 2024. Prepared by the Northfold Health Services Evaluation Unit.
  p.1 Background: Most smokers who try to stop do so without professional help, and specialist stop-smoking clinics reach few of them. Community pharmacies are open long hours and are visited by many smokers, which makes them a promising place to offer structured support.
  p.1 Methods: Twenty-four community pharmacies were randomly allocated to deliver the programme (12 pharmacies) or usual care (12 pharmacies). The programme offered six weekly one-to-one sessions with a trained pharmacy adviser and up to 12 weeks of free varenicline or combination nicotine replacement therapy. Usual care consisted of brief advice and a referral to the council's telephone quitline. The primary outcome was continuous abstinence from smoking at 52 weeks, confirmed by an exhaled carbon monoxide reading below 10 parts per million.
  p.1 Results: Between March 2022 and February 2023, 2,310 adult smokers enrolled, 1,212 at programme pharmacies and 1,098 at usual-care pharmacies. At 52 weeks, 14.2% of programme participants and 8.9% of usual-care participants were abstinent (adjusted odds ratio 1.71, 95% confidence interval 1.26 to 2.32). The programme also increased validated abstinence at four weeks.
  p.1 Conclusions: Structured support from a trained pharmacy adviser, with free stop-smoking medicine, increased long-term quitting compared with brief advice. Community pharmacies are a practical setting for stop-smoking support in Northfold.
  p.2 About 17% of adults in Northfold smoke, above the regional average, and smoking remains the largest single cause of the gap in life expectancy between the most and least deprived parts of the district. The council's specialist stop-smoking clinic sees around 600 smokers a year, a small fraction of those who try to quit. In 2021 the council commissioned a pharmacy-based programme to reach more smokers and asked the Evaluation Unit to test it against usual care before deciding whether to extend it across the district.
  p.2 Evidence on pharmacy-delivered support is mixed. A national audit of pharmacy stop-smoking services found an average four-week quit rate of 35%, although fewer than half of the reported quits were confirmed by carbon monoxide testing (Lomax, 2019). In a cluster trial in 16 pharmacies in Tayford, Ridley and colleagues (2020) reported continuous abstinence at 52 weeks of 11.5% with behavioural support plus nicotine replacement therapy, against 7.2% with brief advice.
  p.2 Medication choice matters. In specialist clinics, varenicline has produced 52-week continuous abstinence of around 23%, compared with 16% for combination nicotine replacement (Ashworth and Nair, 2016). Results for heavier smokers are less consistent: one trial found that smokers of 20 or more cigarettes a day were half as likely as lighter smokers to remain abstinent at 52 weeks (Kerr, 2018), while another found no difference by smoking level (Duval and Haas, 2021). Few trials have reported results separately for older smokers.
  p.3 This was a pragmatic cluster-randomised trial. All 41 community pharmacies in Northfold were invited, and 24 agreed to take part. Pharmacies were randomised in pairs matched on monthly prescription volume and local deprivation, with 12 allocated to the programme and 12 to usual care. Randomisation was carried out by a statistician who had no contact with the pharmacies.
  p.3 Pharmacy staff invited customers who smoked to take part. Adults aged 18 or over who smoked at least five cigarettes a day and wanted to stop within the next month were eligible. Pregnant women were not eligible, because they are referred to the specialist maternity stop-smoking service, and people already using a stop-smoking medicine were also excluded.
  p.3 3.3 Programme and usual care
  p.3 In programme pharmacies, a trained adviser offered six weekly one-to-one sessions of about 20 minutes, starting one week before the quit date. Advisers were pharmacy staff who had completed a two-day accredited training course. Participants chose either varenicline or combination nicotine replacement therapy (a patch plus a short-acting product), supplied free for up to 12 weeks. In usual-care pharmacies, staff gave brief advice and a written referral to the council's telephone quitline, and customers could buy nicotine replacement products as normal.
  p.3 The primary outcome was self-reported continuous abstinence from two weeks after the quit date to 52 weeks, allowing no more than five cigarettes in total, confirmed by an exhaled carbon monoxide reading below 10 parts per million. Secondary outcomes were carbon monoxide-validated abstinence at four weeks and self-reported seven-day abstinence at 26 weeks. Participants lost to follow-up were counted as smokers. Groups were compared with logistic regression adjusted for pharmacy pair, age, sex and cigarettes per day, with standard errors allowing for clustering by pharmacy. Subgroup analyses by cigarettes per day (fewer than 20, or 20 or more) and by sex were specified in advance.
  p.4 Between March 2022 and February 2023, 2,310 smokers enrolled: 1,212 at programme pharmacies and 1,098 at usual-care pharmacies. The two groups were similar at enrolment (Table 1). Participants had a mean age of 44 years, 52% were women, and they smoked a mean of 17 cigarettes a day. Programme pharmacies enrolled a median of 98 participants each and usual-care pharmacies a median of 89. Follow-up at 52 weeks was completed by 78% of programme participants and 73% of usual-care participants.

  p.1 School Streets Pilot Evaluation: Traffic, Air Quality and Travel to School
  p.1 Final report, October 2025. Prepared by the Transport Policy and Research Team, Brackenford Borough Council, with the Centre for Urban Air Research, University of Westmoor.
  p.1 Background. School Streets are timed road closures that restrict motor traffic on the street outside a school at the start and end of the school day. Brackenford Borough Council piloted School Streets at 12 primary schools during the 2024 to 2025 school year.
  p.1 Methods. We compared the pilot period, January to June 2025, with a baseline period covering the same months of 2024. Motor traffic was counted by automatic number plate recognition cameras, nitrogen dioxide (NO2) was measured with diffusion tubes at each school gate and on nearby boundary roads, and travel to school was recorded in hands-up surveys of pupils.
  p.1 Results. Motor traffic on the closed streets fell by 76% during the restriction hours. Mean NO2 at the school gates fell by 14.3%, and the share of pupils walking, cycling or scooting to school rose by nine percentage points. Traffic on the boundary roads rose slightly.
  p.1 Conclusions. The pilot reduced traffic and air pollution outside the schools with little evidence of displacement onto other roads. We recommend that the scheme be made permanent at all 12 sites.
  p.1 Keywords: school streets; timed road closure; nitrogen dioxide; active travel; traffic displacement.
  p.2 Traffic outside schools at drop-off and pick-up times raises concerns about road danger, congestion and children's exposure to air pollution. Children may be particularly vulnerable to traffic-related pollution because they breathe faster than adults and spend time close to the height of vehicle exhausts. Brackenford's 2023 Transport Strategy committed the council to test measures that make the journey to school safer and healthier.
  p.2 This report evaluates the School Streets pilot, which began in September 2024. It sets out the effects of the pilot on motor traffic in the closed streets, on NO2 concentrations, on how pupils travel to school and on traffic in the wider road network, and it reports the views of parents and residents. The report is intended to inform the council's decision on whether to make the scheme permanent.
  p.2 The pilot forms part of a wider programme to reduce car use for short journeys in the borough. Most primary pupils in Brackenford live within walking distance of their school, yet many are driven, and head teachers have reported repeated complaints about parking on pavements and across driveways at the start and end of the school day.
  p.2 2 Background and previous studies
  p.2 School Streets have spread rapidly since 2017, and a growing number of evaluations have been published. In a study of 37 schemes in a large capital city, Rowland and Tait (2021) reported that NO2 at the school gate fell by up to 23% during the morning drop-off period. Kerrigan and colleagues (2022) studied 18 sites in northern England and found that traffic on boundary roads rose by 4% on average, with no measurable change in NO2 on those roads.
  p.2 Effects on travel behaviour have also varied. Abbott (2020) reported that the share of pupils driven to school fell from 31% to 24% across a programme of 22 schools, while Pereira and Lund (2022) found no change in car use at schools where the closures were staffed by volunteers rather than enforced by cameras. Daley and Moss (2023) reviewed 14 evaluations and found that parental support for making schemes permanent ranged from 63% to 81%.
  p.2 Most published studies have been short, have lacked a comparison period in the same months of the year, or have measured air quality at only one or two sites. The present evaluation was designed to address these gaps by using a full baseline period and by monitoring at every pilot school.
  p.3 The evaluation used a before-and-after design with matched calendar months. The baseline period ran from January to June 2024 and the pilot period from January to June 2025, so that seasonal differences in weather and traffic were balanced. The 12 participating primary schools were selected from 31 schools that applied, on the basis of traffic volume, road layout and the agreement of the head teacher.
  p.3 At each school, the street outside the main entrance was closed to motor traffic from 08:15 to 09:15 and from 14:45 to 15:45 on school days. Residents, blue badge holders and essential services could apply for an exemption. The closures were enforced by automatic number plate recognition cameras, and drivers without an exemption received a warning letter during the first four weeks and a penalty charge notice after that. Signs and planters marked the closure points, and school staff were asked not to act as marshals.
  p.3 Motor vehicles entering each closed street during the restriction hours were counted by the enforcement cameras on every school day. Traffic on eight boundary roads, the main roads to which diverted vehicles were expected to move, was counted with pneumatic tube counters for two weeks in each month. The tube counters were checked against manual counts on one morning in each month.
  p.3 NO2 was measured with passive diffusion tubes exposed for one month at a time at the gate of each school, at the eight boundary road sites and at three urban background sites away from main roads. Results were bias-adjusted using a co-location study at the council's reference monitoring station. Continuous monitors that record hourly NO2 values were also installed at four schools.
  p.3 Pupils' usual mode of travel to school was recorded with a hands-up survey in each class in March 2024 and March 2025. Parents, and residents living within 200 metres of a pilot school, were invited to complete an online survey in May 2025.
